facts.claim: Katie Pruitt's "Ohio" is a cover of a Neil Young song, first released by Crosby, Stills, Nash & Young in 1970.
The two-song single "Ohio / After The Gold Rush" came out on October 29, 2020, on Rounder Records (distributed by Concord). "Ohio" runs 3:21.

Credits for Pruitt's "Ohio": Katie Pruitt (vocals, producer), Hank Born (guitar), Jess Nolan (background vocals), Calvin Knowles (bass) and Ross McReynolds (drums). Gary Paczosa is the recording engineer.
AllMusic credits Pruitt and Gary Paczosa as producers of the single. It lists Jess Nolan on keyboards and background vocals, and Neil Young as composer.
Pruitt recorded "Ohio" shortly after returning home, on the same day as her original "Look The Other Way" and the Neil Young cover "After the Gold Rush".
Northern Transmissions describes the original "Ohio" as Young's angry response to the May 1970 Kent State shootings. It says Pruitt released her cover five days before the November 2020 election.
Pruitt sees "Ohio" as having a double meaning in 2020. It serves as an anthem against police brutality, and it acknowledges the roughly 230,000 Americans who had died of coronavirus.
Pruitt played "Ohio" live, followed by "After the Gold Rush", at a Nashville show at The Basement on October 25, 2020. The reviewer noted that studio versions were then released as a single.
The single followed her Rounder debut album Expectations, released in February 2020. It was also released shortly after her original protest song "Look The Other Way".
Pruitt grew up in suburban Atlanta and began writing songs as a teenager. She was first drawn to rock and punk bands, then to Joni Mitchell and Bonnie Raitt, and she moved to Nashville for college.

research.lineage: Pruitt's "Ohio" belongs to the tradition of 1970s Neil Young protest songs, reinterpreted by a Nashville folk-rock/Americana singer-songwriter whose work blends rock grit with folk storytelling.

draft:
The line that does the work in **Ohio** isn't the one everybody knows. It's the question in the middle: "What if you knew her and / Found her dead on the ground?" Neil Young wrote it in 1970, after the Kent State shootings, as an angry dare to anyone keeping their distance. In Katie Pruitt's hands it becomes a test of empathy. The song refuses to let the dead stay abstract. It asks you to put a face you love on the ground and then tells you what you already know, that running isn't an option once you've pictured it.

Pruitt released the cover five days before the November 2020 election, and she has said the song carried a double meaning that year. It worked as an anthem against police brutality, and it marked the roughly 230,000 Americans who had died of coronavirus by then. That reading changes what "Four dead in Ohio" means. The number stays four, but the grief behind it gets much bigger. The original was a newspaper headline set to a riff. Pruitt sings it as a stand-in for every count that kept rising that year.

The arrangement doesn't rough the song up the way Crosby, Stills, Nash & Young did. An acoustic guitar picks out arpeggiated chords. An electric guitar, played by Hank Born, holds a clean, sustained melody line. Calvin Knowles walks the bass underneath, and Ross McReynolds keeps a steady, driving beat with the snare out front. The production is clean and polished, with space around the players. Pruitt's voice is clear with a slight rasp, and the delivery is direct. There's no snarl in it. The anger comes through as steadiness, the sound of someone who has decided to say this plainly and keep saying it.

That steadiness fits the lyric's structure. The wordless "na, na-na-na" stretch is a crowd's chant, the part anyone can join in on. The ending repeats "Four dead in Ohio" seven times, and it lands less like a hook than a roll call that won't stop.

Pruitt grew up in suburban Atlanta loving rock and punk before turning to Joni Mitchell and Bonnie Raitt, and both pulls show here: the punk kid's belief that a song can be a weapon, the songwriter's trust in a clear voice over noise. She recorded it shortly after returning home, on the same day as her own protest song "Look The Other Way" and a cover of Young's "After the Gold Rush." Hearing it, you can tell she meant it as part of the same argument.

The song gets under your skin by making you imagine one specific person on the ground, and then counting, over and over, until the number feels like a name.
